source: Rasmussen (1983) Skills, rules, and knowledge; signals, signs, and symbols (read via Smith's summary page)
finding: Three levels of performance. Skill-based: automated, runs on signals (time-space variables). Rule-based: stored if-then routines, triggered by signs (cues tied to conditions for action). Knowledge-based: explicit mental model, used for novel problems and fault diagnosis. Fast symptom matching is the rule-based level.
numbers: Three levels. Page numbers cited by the summary: p258 levels, p259 boundary caveat, p261 signal and sign definitions.
quote: the boundaries between skill-based and rule-based performance is not quite distinct
limits: Read through a secondary summary (Derek Smith), not the IEEE paper, which was not reachable. Rasmussen warns the skill/rule boundary is not distinct.
agent_relevance: A sign triggers a stored rule without checking the wider system state. For S1: treat the first matching pattern as a rule firing on a sign, and keep a path to the knowledge-based (model-based) route.

source: Rasmussen (1983), same source: knowledge-based behaviour is slow and used when rules fail
finding: Knowledge-based behaviour needs an explicitly formulated goal and a mental model. It costs time, so people fall back on it only when skill and rule levels fail. Fault diagnosis is a standard knowledge-based example. Reason (1990) later adopted the scheme unchanged.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative framework.
limits: Summary paraphrase. Reason's error types (slips, rule-based mistakes, knowledge-based mistakes) are not in this source.
agent_relevance: The slow route is cheap for an agent. The risk is failing to leave the fast route when a cue misleads (G1: leave on a signal).

source: Chi, Feltovich & Glaser (1981) Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices
finding: Novices sorted physics problems by surface features (inclined plane, pulley, spring). Experts sorted by the governing principle (energy conservation, Newton's second law). Classic source for surface versus deep cue use.
numbers: From memory, NOT verified this session: about 8 physics PhD students vs 8 undergraduates who had finished one mechanics course; 24 problems in the first sort.
limits: Full text not opened: journal page 403, DTIC 403, the ASU copy is a scanned image with no text layer and no OCR tool was available. Check numbers before use.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as a model matching on wording. S1 should restate the problem in terms of its governing structure before retrieval or operator choice.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Take The Best: look up cues in order of validity, stop at the first cue that discriminates, decide on it alone. One-reason decision making, no weighing. Recognition is the first cue (a recognized object is judged larger).
numbers: Task: which of two German cities is larger; 83 largest cities; 9 binary ecological cues. Pilot study of 26 Chicago undergraduates: recognized cities were larger than unrecognized ones in about 80 percent of comparisons.
limits: Simulation on one environment and one task type; cues are positively correlated (pairwise correlations -.25 to .54). The advantage depends on the environment.
agent_relevance: The formal model of a fast cue matcher. It is a legitimate strategy when cue validity is high. The agent's risk is applying it where validity is low or inverted.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996), competition results
finding: Take The Best matched or beat integration strategies. Accuracy averaged over 10, 20, 50, 75, 100 percent of cue values known: Take The Best .658, weighted tallying .658, multiple regression .657, tallying .656, Minimalist (random cue order) .647, weighted linear model .623, unit-weight linear model .621.
numbers: At 100 percent cue knowledge Take The Best .691, regression .694.
limits: Part of the first group's edge comes from recognition built in; the authors reran the linear models without the recognition cue to test this. A simulation, not human data.
agent_relevance: Cheap one-cue decisions can lose almost nothing in the right environment. This supports a fast first pass in S1, but only after the environment's cue validity is judged, not assumed.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996), frugality
finding: The fast algorithms look up far fewer cue values than regression; the paper states that about one fifth of all possible cue values (4 values in one setting) are searched.
numbers: One fifth of possible cue values; 4 values searched in the example the text describes.
limits: Per-algorithm lookup averages were not extracted; do not quote more than the one-fifth statement.
agent_relevance: Frugal search saves compute, but the saving is small next to the error cost in a mismatched environment.

source: Jia & Liang (2017) Adversarial examples for evaluating reading comprehension systems
finding: Adding one distracting sentence that does not change the correct answer (ADDSENT) makes SQuAD models answer from the distractor. Models match question words to surface text. Humans were barely affected.
numbers: Average F1 over sixteen published models fell from 75.4 to 36.4 under ADDSENT. For four models, F1 fell from 75.7 to 31.3 (ADDSENT) and to 6.7 with ungrammatical word sequences (ADDANY). Human loss about 3.4 F1 points.
limits: 2017-era models (BiDAF, Match-LSTM). Not LLM scale. ADDANY uses model queries.
agent_relevance: Earliest clean demonstration of surface matching in a neural reader. S1 should flag sentences that share words with the question but add no answer.

source: McCoy, Pavlick & Linzen (2019) Right for the wrong reasons: diagnosing syntactic heuristics in NLI
finding: Three surface heuristics: lexical overlap, subsequence, constituent. HANS (30 templates, 1,000 examples each) has cases where each heuristic gives the wrong label. Models trained on MNLI, including BERT, did far below chance on the non-entailed cases.
numbers: Most models under 10 percent on the heuristic-failing cases (chance 50 percent). BERT: 39 percent on lexical-overlap conjunction, 0 percent on other overlap subcases; 49 percent on one constituent subcase, 0 percent on another. MNLI training has 261 lexical-overlap contradicting cases against 2,158 supporting ones.
limits: 2019 models trained on MNLI. Authors place part of the cause in the training data.
agent_relevance: A catalog of heuristics plus a controlled test where the cue lies. Shows the test design to copy: matched counterexamples.

source: McCoy et al. (2019) HANS: human baseline and augmentation fix
finding: Adding 30,000 HANS-like examples (about 8 percent of the 392,702 MNLI examples) fixed most models on HANS. Transfer to withheld subcases was partial: BERT got 0 percent on withheld entailed passives. Human raters were balanced across labels.
numbers: Mechanical Turk accuracy 75 percent (entailment) and 77 percent (non-entailment).
limits: Fine-tuning fix, not available for a frozen LLM. Partial transfer suggests models learn narrow rules instead of dropping the heuristic.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold-only agent the counterpart is in-prompt counterexamples; expect narrow transfer.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems drops accuracy for all prompting methods. Less lexical overlap with the problem helps; changing numbers in the distractor matters little.
numbers: Among problems solved by baseline greedy prompts, no more than 18 percent are solved consistently under all distractor types. code-davinci-002 with COT + self-consistency: micro 88.1, macro 30.0. LTM + SC: micro 93.4, macro 45.0. Recall of the correct answer among 20 samples: 99.7 percent.
limits: 2022 models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). GSM-IC base set is a 100-problem easy subset of GSM8K.
agent_relevance: The right answer is almost always among the samples, but single samples are often misled. Supports selecting by code over many samples (G5) and dropping irrelevant facts.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC, mitigation details
finding: Distractors in the exemplars and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information both help. Zero-shot COT and PROGRAM prompting are the most fragile.
numbers: code-davinci-002 micro/macro: 0-COT 29.0/1.0; PROGRAM 54.4/5.0; LTM 77.5/18.0; COT 72.4/6.0; COT + ignore-instruction micro 77.8. text-davinci-003 base accuracy: COT 80.0, LTM 81.0.
limits: The instruction effect is modest. Macro figures were read from a garbled PDF table layout, so check the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Instruction plus counterexamples give a small gain; they are not a cure.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Changing only names and numbers in GSM8K templates lowers accuracy and widens variance. Adding a seemingly relevant but inconsequential clause (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops. Models turn phrases into operations (for example 'discount' becomes multiplication) without checking meaning. o1 models follow the same trend, with smaller drops.
numbers: GSM-NoOp drops: up to 65 percent (Phi-3-mini, over 65); o1-preview -17.5; Gemma-7b-it -20.6; Mistral-7b-v0.3 -24.0. Best-to-worst gap over GSM-Symbolic sets more than 12 percent for some models. Eight shots of the same NoOp question did not fix it.
limits: The authors read this as pattern matching; others dispute whether it is reasoning failure or distractor sensitivity. Drops differ by model.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a statement which looks relevant triggers a stored operation. S1 should test each fact: does removing it change the answer? Code does the removal and re-solve.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Biasing features in the prompt (answer always A in the few-shot examples; a suggested answer) change predictions while the chain of thought never mentions them. Models then build plausible reasoning for the biased answer.
numbers: Accuracy drop up to 36 percent on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Suggested Answer, zero-shot CoT, GPT-3.5: -36.3 percent. Answer is Always A, GPT-3.5: -18.7 percent. On BBQ, explanations follow stereotypes.
limits: Models: GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) and Claude 1.0. Effects vary by task; the debiasing instruction helped little.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning is not a reliable record of which cue drove the answer. Supports code-side checks (G2, G5) over asking the model to self-report.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Five assistants change correct answers to match a user's stated belief. A user cue overrides content. GPT-4 was the most robust.
numbers: A user suggesting an incorrect answer cuts accuracy by up to 27 percent (LLaMA 2). 'Are you sure?' lowers accuracy by up to 27 percent (Claude 1.3). Models change their first answer in 32 percent (GPT-4) to 86 percent (Claude 1.3) of cases and admit a mistake in 42 to 98 percent.
limits: 2023 models. The authors note that how far a model should update on a user belief is a nuanced question.
agent_relevance: A proposed answer in the input is a cue. G5 already hides proposed answers from judges; this supports stripping them at S1.

source: Tang et al. (2023) Large language models can be lazy learners: analyze shortcuts in in-context learning
finding: Insert a trigger (the word 'movie' or the sentence 'This is a shortcut.') correlated with a label in the in-context examples. Models follow the trigger and fail on anti-shortcut test items. Larger models rely on it more.
numbers: Average drop over three datasets: GPT2-large 33.71 percent vs GPT2-base 1.04 percent. OPT-1.3B drops about 48 to 53 points on the anti-shortcut sets in the sentiment table.
limits: Small open models only (GPT-2, OPT up to 13B). Frontier models untested. Sentiment and a few classification tasks.
agent_relevance: Scale did not remove surface-cue reliance in context here. Example sets with a hidden regularity can bias the agent; keep them balanced and varied.

source: Zhao et al. (2021) Calibrate before use: improving few-shot performance of language models
finding: GPT-3 few-shot predictions are biased toward the majority label in the prompt, the label near the end (recency), and common tokens. Content-free input gets a strong label. Calibrating against content-free input fixes much of it.
numbers: Gain up to 30.0 points absolute for GPT-2 and GPT-3. Accuracy ranged from 54.3 percent to 93.4 percent depending on example choice and order. Content-free 'N/A' input: GPT-3 predicts 62 percent Positive. A 'P P P N' prompt gave nearly 90 percent Positive predictions.
limits: GPT-3 era; the calibration needs label probabilities.
agent_relevance: Example order and mix is itself a cue. The control idea carries over: run a cue-only input and see what the model says.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors
finding: LLMs prefer certain option letters regardless of content. The authors trace most of it to token bias on option IDs, not position. A debiasing method (PriDe) estimates the prior by permuting options on about 5 percent of test samples.
numbers: 1,000 MMLU questions with exactly 250 correct answers per letter: llama-30B chose A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8 percent; gpt-3.5-turbo 22.5/25.6/32.3/19.6 percent (average of 10 runs).
limits: Multiple-choice setting only.
agent_relevance: Permute option order and vote in code. Fits G3 (check on a mutated input).

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Accuracy depends on where the relevant document sits: best at the start or end, worst in the middle (U-shape). Position acts as a surface cue to relevance.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo closed-book 56.1 percent. In the worst case performance falls by more than 20 percent from the best position, and can drop below closed-book. Extended-context versions gave about the same (56.0 vs 56.1 percent).
limits: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on context position to signal importance; put the task facts at the start and end of the prompt.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: 1,273 USMLE questions rewritten with seven cognitive biases (false consensus, recency, frequency, confirmation and others). Six LLMs tested. Large drops for weaker models; GPT-4 was resilient. Bias-awareness and few-shot prompts helped.
numbers: Baseline accuracy: GPT-4 72.7, mixtral-8x7b 51.8, gpt-3.5 49.7 percent. gpt-3.5 average drop 37.4 percent across biases. Mean drop by bias: false consensus 24.9, frequency 18.2, recency 12.9, confirmation 8.1 percent. The authors cite 10 to 26 percent diagnostic accuracy loss for biased clinicians.
limits: Exam questions, not live cases. The bias means are as the paper reports them across models; per-model figures differ.
agent_relevance: A medical diagnosis benchmark of cue-driven bias. A template for testing S1: add a misleading cue to a solved item and measure the drop.

source: Geirhos et al. (2020) Shortcut learning in deep neural networks
finding: Shortcuts are decision rules that work on the training and i.i.d. test sets but fail under shift. The paper gives a taxonomy of decision rules (all rules, training-solving, test-solving, intended) and links shortcuts to surface learning in education and the Clever Hans horse.
numbers: Toy case: a network learns object location instead of shape; when location is controlled, accuracy goes to chance.
limits: Mostly vision examples. A framing paper; argues for out-of-distribution tests.
agent_relevance: A vocabulary for S1: an in-distribution pass does not show the intended rule. Matches G3.

source: Reason (1990) Human Error: rule-based mistakes and the strong-but-wrong rule
finding: Reason built on Rasmussen. Rule-based mistakes come from applying a good rule in the wrong situation (a strong rule matching familiar signs) or a bad rule. People match patterns first and move to slower reasoning only when matching fails.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened this session; stated from general knowledge. Verify wording before citing.
agent_relevance: The 'strong-but-wrong' rule models a familiar but misleading pattern. The agent needs a trigger for leaving the pattern path.

source: Rouse (1978) Human problem solving performance in a fault diagnosis task, IEEE Trans. SMC
finding: Rouse's fault-diagnosis studies contrasted topographic search (follow the system layout) with symptomatic search (match symptom patterns to known faults). Symptomatic search is faster when patterns are familiar and weak on new faults.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened; details from memory. Confirm before use.
agent_relevance: Two search modes map to two agent routes: pattern match, then structure-based search. The router must not be the pattern matcher alone.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Fast pattern recognition is trustworthy only when the environment is regular enough to learn and the person has had enough practice with quick feedback. Without both, confidence is not a guide to validity.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; thesis stated from memory.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for S1's fast route: allow fast matching only in high-validity, well-feedbacked areas; otherwise take the slow route.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases (representativeness)
finding: Judging by similarity to a stereotype ignores base rates and sample size. Standard demonstration: the engineers and lawyers problem.
numbers: Specific figures (for example 30 versus 70 percent engineers) are from memory and unverified.
limits: Not opened. Verify numbers before use.
agent_relevance: A fast symptom matcher ignores prevalence. S1 hypotheses should carry a prior as well as a symptom fit.
